turns.answer_text:
**My recommendation is a near-stoichiometric Y–Ba–Cu–O composition as a conservative, data-supported high-\(T_c\) candidate—not a certified robust global maximum.** The supplied data do not establish any composition’s performance under every ±5% single-variable perturbation.

### What the data support

The strongest evidence for a repeatable high-\(T_c\) region among the permitted elements is around **YBa₂Cu₃O₇**:

| Composition | Observed \(T_c\) (K) |
|---|---:|
| YBa₂Cu₃O₆.₈₂ | 89.9 |
| YBa₂Cu₃O₆.₈₇ | 93.5 |
| YBa₂Cu₃O₆.₉₅ | 92.8 |
| YBa₂Cu₃O₆.₉₆ | 92.3 |
| YBa₂Cu₃O₇ | 83.0, 90.2 |

These observations favor a **region near 90 K**, rather than relying on one unusually high measurement. They also show measurement or processing variability: identical recorded compositions need not have identical \(T_c\).

Higher permitted-element observations exist—for example, `Ba2Ca2Cu3O` at 126 K—but that isolated record provides no evidence of a broad optimum. Its unusually low recorded oxygen stoichiometry also warrants verification before using it as an optimization target. I would not extrapolate a robust 126 K prediction from it.

### Proposed composition and robustness limitation

I recommend **YBa₂Cu₃O₆.₉₅**, normalized to elemental fractions. All fractions satisfy your bounds and sum to one. I avoid adding dopants because several nearby Zn-, Pr-, and other substituted records have substantially lower \(T_c\).

A reasonable **observational expectation is approximately 90 K**, not a validated prediction interval. Importantly, the nearby observations cover oxygen changes much smaller than the requested ±5% test. Thus, this candidate still requires perturbation experiments; claiming that it already satisfies your no-collapse requirement would overstate the evidence.

For those experiments, vary one elemental amount by ±5%, then renormalize all fractions to sum to one. Zero-valued elements remain zero under a relative perturbation; testing contamination requires a separate absolute threshold.
